text: to investigate the impact of adaptive lighting in a real- world scenario. The City of Cambridge, Massachusetts, utilizes an adaptive approach to their lighting system. At various times, based on the road category and the locations, the lighting dims. This project considered the implications of this dimming approach to the lighting system. 4.1 Methodology This project applied a three-step methodology. The first step was a deep analysis of the ALS implemented in the field, including a review of crash and crime statistics, lighting data, and the collection of public opinion on the ALS. Additionally, the system was compared to the lighting in the adjacent city of Somerset, which has comparable demographics. The second step involved bringing focus groups together where roadway lighting practitioners could share their impressions of and approaches to adaptive lighting. The final step was to survey the public on their impressions of adaptive lighting. The surveys were conducted both in Cambridge and Somerville. 4.1.1 Test Location Cambridge, Massachusetts, is a suburb of Boston and is the fourth-largest city in Massachusetts, with a population of 118,403 as of 2020. Cambridge includes both Harvard and MIT universities and is a hub for the development of technology innovation. Cambridge replaced approximately 7,000 lights (4,900 streetlights and 2,100 in specialty and park fixtures) with LEDs and installed a control system for each of the luminaires. As part of the development of the ALS, the city analyzed the lighting needs in zones and determined the appropriate lighting level for the zone. They then developed criteria for dimming based on roadway type and usage by pedestrians and vehicles. When the usage drops below a certain level, the lighting system can be dimmed. The analysis determined the time of day for dimming, which then determined the dimming algorithm. Based on available literature, Cambridge started testing the LED lighting system on a small number of roadway segments from 2010 to 2013. Although not specified, it appeared that full- scale citywide replacement on streets and parks later took place in 2014 and 2015 (Cambridge, 2014), City of Cambridge, n.d.). Initially, the newly installed LED systems were set at 70% of their initial brightness to account for light deterioration over time. In addition, the light systems are dimmed to 50% of their normal brightness “later in the evening” and further to about a third of their current brightness “by the time most of us are going to bed.” (Cambridge, n.d.) The lighting levels for the roads were selected in two ways. The first was roadway class. They characterized the roadway as a C1 through C3 category, where C1 are major state-maintained roadways, C2 are mostly state-maintained roadways with a portion of major local roads, and C3 consists of only local roadways that are not included in the state Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS) network. The second criteria for lighting selection was that of 33 pedestrian usage, which was categorized as high, medium, or low through a P class designation.
